candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — beta-lactam allergy assessment
candidate.educational_objective: When ceftriaxone is considered for a client with a penicillin-allergy label, characterize the prior reaction and use reaction severity and type to guide risk assessment rather than assuming universal avoidance or universal safety.

options.A: Any reported penicillin allergy requires permanent avoidance of every cephalosporin regardless of the reaction history.
options.B: The prior reaction should be characterized; third-generation cephalosporins have low cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy, while high-risk histories require additional evaluation.
options.C: The allergy history can be ignored because penicillins and cephalosporins have no clinically relevant relationship.
options.D: Ceftriaxone is automatically safe after any severe delayed beta-lactam reaction because those reactions do not affect future beta-lactam use.

candidate.rationale: CDC guidance recommends obtaining a thorough allergy history and notes that third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone have low cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy. High-risk histories, including anaphylaxis or severe cutaneous/non-IgE reactions, require a different approach and may warrant avoidance or allergy referral. Therefore B is the best answer. A is overly broad, C incorrectly dismisses beta-lactam cross-reactivity, and D conflicts with CDC guidance for severe delayed reactions.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone have low cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy; evaluation begins with a thorough allergy history, and severe IgE or non-IgE histories require more cautious management or referral.
